clue.text: First of the States to restrict new pubs

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter, so only that letter is kept

parts.note: opening letter of the word

indicators.note: to restrict something is to hem it in, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: to state is to aver, so he states = he avers
N is the standard abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A US state passes a law limiting the opening of new bars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'States' looks like American states, but it is the verb: avers. The N sits inside AVERS, after the T.
explanation.definitionFit: Taverns are inns or bars serving drinks, a plain synonym for pubs in everyday usage.

clue.text: Understood 16 across broadcast (excluding Northern Ireland)

indicators.note: broadcast seed is scattered widely, so the letters are strewn into a new order
excluding something means leaving it out, so those letters are removed

parts.note: the answer to 16 across, the film
NI is the usual abbreviation for Northern Ireland

explanation.surface: Someone grasps a film being shown on TV, apart from in Northern Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: Take N and I out of TITANIC to leave TITAC, then rearrange those five letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Tacit agreement is implied without being stated aloud, so it is merely understood rather than spoken.

clue.text: He scored six with just one dropped

parts.note: Roman numeral for six

indicators.note: in a down clue a dropped letter falls lower in the column, which reorders the word it belongs to

parts.note: a just or sound argument is valid

explanation.surface: A cricketer hit a six despite one catch being dropped.
explanation.walkthrough: The I (one) of VALID drops one place down the column to give VALDI. 'Scored' sounds like cricket runs, but it means wrote music.
explanation.definitionFit: Antonio Vivaldi composed The Four Seasons, and to score is to write a musical score, so he is a man who scored.

clue.text: Bloody hell — gross national product taking just seconds to bounce back

indicators.note: something that bounces back returns the way it came, so the string runs in the opposite direction
only the seconds means keeping nothing but the second letter of each word

parts.note: second letter
second letter
second letter
second letter

explanation.surface: An exasperated economist curses as the GNP takes a brief dip before recovering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloody hell' reads as one oath, but 'Bloody' alone is the definition, in the steak sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A rare steak is cooked briefly and still red and bloody inside, the butcher's or cook's sense.

clue.text: Hint to cut some habit at the beach?

definitions.meaning: setter's reading: the answer itself, read as a clue, tells you to rearrange the letters of 'cut some', its first word being an anagram signal
surface reading: clothing worn on the sand, a habit being a garment

explanation.surface: A tip for trimming some of a monk's robe down to something fit for the seaside.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a reverse clue: the first word of the answer is a common anagram signal and the second is a rearrangement of 'cut some', so the answer is a hint for solving those words.
explanation.definitionFit: A habit is a garment, as a nun's habit is, and a bathing suit is the garment people wear at the seaside.

clue.text: Not many working early to late, say

indicators.note: letters that are working are being worked over, kneaded into a fresh order

parts.note: the letters taken as printed

explanation.surface: Few people keep working all day, from early morning to late at night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Early to late' looks like working hours, but it is an example: one word set against its opposite. 'Say' marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Early is the opposite word of late, so the pair illustrate the relation of opposite meanings between words.

clue.text: Throughout Los Angeles hills, ants ultimately stripped ground

indicators.note: ground material is crushed and broken up, so the letters are reduced and reformed
'ultimately' points to a final letter, and stripping it out wherever it appears removes it entirely

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written; its last letter is the one stripped out everywhere

explanation.surface: All over the hills of Los Angeles, the ants have stripped the earth bare.
explanation.walkthrough: The last letter of 'ants' is S; remove every S from 'Los Angeles hills ants' and the fifteen letters left rearrange into the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means at every point or in every respect, so it is a phrasal equivalent of throughout.

clue.text: Clairvoyant's lie that collapses assuming recording caught …

indicators.note: to assume is to take on, so one piece takes another inside it
a structure that collapses falls into a jumble, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
an EP is an extended-play record
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A psychic's fib falls apart once a recording catches them out.
explanation.walkthrough: Rearrange LIE THAT as TELATHI, slip EP inside it, then add C. The ellipsis just carries the sentence on into the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe someone with supposed psychic powers, perceiving things beyond the normal senses.

clue.text: … name provided on stage quicker

indicators.note: in a down clue one thing on another sits above it, so the earlier pieces are placed first

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for name
provided that = if
a stage or level is a tier

explanation.surface: Continuing the psychic theme: the name comes to them more quickly on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links the clue to the one before, but the two are solved separately. 'Stage' suggests theatre, but it is a level.
explanation.definitionFit: Nifty means agile and nimble as well as neat, so a niftier mover is a faster one.

clue.text: Ruin sex and — essentially — what's left of marriage

parts.note: to mar is to spoil or ruin
'it' is a coy word for sex

indicators.note: the essence of something is its core, so only the central letter is kept

parts.note: the central letter of the word
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A gloomy view: wrecked sex life and the essence of a marriage is all that remains.
explanation.walkthrough: The dashes make 'essentially' look like an aside on the whole sentence; it applies only to the word after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Marital is the adjective for things relating to husband and wife, so it means pertaining to wedlock.

clue.text: Model cake's good in real life

parts.note: to cake something in mud is to cover it
G is the abbreviation for good
IRL is texting shorthand for in real life

explanation.surface: A model maker's cake turns out tasty when actually eaten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cake' is a verb here, as in boots caked in mud; the 's stands for 'has' joining the two halves.
explanation.definitionFit: A cover girl is a woman photographed for a magazine front, a particular kind of fashion model.

clue.text: Prisoner appearing in twisted feature film

indicators.note: twisted round, the letters face the other way and are read backwards
something appearing in a phrase is found inside it, sitting within the run of letters

parts.note: the letters spanning the two words

explanation.surface: A convict stars in a crime movie with a twisty plot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twisted' looks like a review of the film's plot, but it tells you to read the hidden letters backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A lifer is slang for someone serving a life sentence in jail, a specific kind of convict.

clue.text: 14 to follow story

indicators.note: the cross-reference makes this 'listen to', and listening means you go by sound rather than spelling

parts.note: to follow someone covertly is to tail them

explanation.surface: Someone is told to listen in order to follow a story.
explanation.walkthrough: Replace 14 with its answer, LISTEN, and the instruction reads 'listen to follow'.
explanation.definitionFit: A tale is a narrative account, real or invented, a direct synonym for a story.

clue.text: Shopping centre advertising in street outside — most people ignore it

indicators.note: a piece outside another wraps around it, holding the rest between its letters

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street
a shopping centre is a mall
PR is public relations, promotion
taken as written

explanation.surface: Billboards outside a shopping mall that passers-by never look at.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Most people ignore it' reads as a comment on the adverts, but it is the whole definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The fine terms and conditions at the bottom of a contract are notoriously skipped by almost everyone who signs.

clue.text: Perhaps Olive and Ruby maybe able to hold game

parts.note: a ruby is an example of a precious stone

indicators.note: to hold something is to grip it inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: fit and able
RU is rugby union

explanation.surface: Two women, Olive and Ruby, might be fit enough to take part in a game.
explanation.walkthrough: Olive and Ruby look like two names, but one is a fruit and the other a gem.
explanation.definitionFit: An olive has a single hard pit inside its flesh, like a plum or cherry, so it is an example of a drupe.

clue.text: Pay attention — nothing's holding French and Saunders' finale back

indicators.note: going back means travelling in the opposite direction, so the whole string is read right to left
a piece holding others contains them within its letters

parts.note: nil is nothing, zero
et is French for and

indicators.note: a finale is the closing part, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: final letter of the name

explanation.surface: A comedy fan is told to pay attention: nothing is holding up the end of a French and Saunders show.
explanation.walkthrough: French and Saunders were a British comedy double act, so the pair read as one name; split them and 'French and' becomes a translation. The 's after 'nothing' stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: To listen is to give heed with the ears, the same request as paying attention to someone.

clue.text: Note planet discovered by a student is untouched by human hand

indicators.note: dis-covered means having its covering removed, so the outer letters go

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for note
the ringed sixth planet
taken as written
L is a learner, as on a learner driver's plate

explanation.surface: A record that a student found a new planet, still pristine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discovered' suggests finding the planet, but it means stripping off its first and last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Natural things exist in nature without manufacture or human interference, so they are untouched by people.

clue.text: Film about hot American singer making a comeback

indicators.note: a comeback is a return, so the letters travel back the way they came

parts.note: C is circa, about
what is hot is fashionable, in
A is the abbreviation for American
a songbird, here the small garden bird

explanation.surface: A movie about a sexy American vocalist's return to the stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'American singer' wants to be a named US star, but the singer is a bird and American just A.
explanation.definitionFit: Titanic is the 1997 James Cameron movie about the doomed ocean liner, a specific example of a motion picture.

clue.text: Bear advanced — I'm ready to shoot

definitions.note: the answer is a verb phrase, 'get ready to shoot'

parts.note: to bear a load is to take it
A is the abbreviation for advanced
taken as written

explanation.surface: A hunter faces an approaching bear and says they are ready to fire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bear' looks like the hunter's target, but it is the verb meaning to carry or take.
explanation.definitionFit: Pointing a weapon at a target is the final preparation before firing, so it describes getting set to shoot.

clue.text: Worry one isn't exercising

indicators.note: exercising puts things through their paces and moves them about, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters taken as printed

explanation.surface: A fitness worry: a person is fretting about skipping the gym.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'isn’t' is ignored, leaving seven letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Tension is mental strain and nervous anxiety, which overlaps closely with worry as a noun.

clue.text: Nurse's job? Get air supply

indicators.note: read as 'supple-y', in a supple, bending way, so the letters flex into a new order

parts.note: the letters taken as printed

explanation.surface: A nurse's role is to make sure the patient gets an oxygen supply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply' looks like a noun, as in air supply, but it is the adverb from supple. The question mark flags that sorting patients is one example of nursing work.
explanation.definitionFit: Triage is sorting casualties by urgency on arrival, a task often done by emergency-department nurses.

clue.text: Player of golf round stood to make this kind of bread?

indicators.note: going round something encircles it, so one piece is put around the other

parts.note: Gary Player is a South African golfing great
a candidate who stood for election ran

explanation.surface: A golfer has stood for a round and somehow ends up baking a loaf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Player' is the golfer's surname, so the clue wants his first name. Granary is a British brand-name brown loaf with malted whole grains.
explanation.definitionFit: Granary bread is a malted wholemeal loaf with grains in it, a particular type sold in UK bakeries.

clue.text: One's brilliant with Wings, Elvis and Queen on bass for example

indicators.note: in an across clue one thing on another follows it, so the earlier-named piece is placed second

parts.note: Elvis Presley was the King of rock and roll
a bass is a kind of fish
ER is Elizabeth Regina

explanation.surface: A music fan raves about Wings, Elvis and Queen, with the bass playing as an example.
explanation.walkthrough: Wings, Elvis and Queen read as a list of pop acts, but Wings belongs to the definition, and the bass is a fish, not a guitar.
explanation.definitionFit: The kingfisher is a bird with dazzling blue and orange plumage, so it is a winged creature that is brilliant.

clue.text: Welshman capturing El Salvador?

definitions.note: a forename standing for the man

indicators.note: a captor holds a captive inside, so one piece is held within the other

parts.note: Dai is a stock Welsh man's name
'el' is how the letter L is spelt out

explanation.surface: A Welsh soldier seizes the Central American country of El Salvador.
explanation.walkthrough: 'El Salvador' reads as the country, but it splits: El is the letter, Salvador the painter's first name, and the question mark admits the trick.
explanation.definitionFit: Salvador Dalí was the Spanish surrealist painter, so his first name stands for the man himself.

clue.text: Italy was first after Germany did nothing

indicators.note: coming after means following on, so the later piece is placed behind the earlier one

parts.note: I is the international vehicle code for Italy
D is the international vehicle code for Germany (Deutschland)
to be first is to lead

explanation.surface: A sporting tale: Italy took the lead when Germany failed to respond.
explanation.walkthrough: Italy's I comes first; LED is placed after D.
explanation.definitionFit: To idle is to be inactive and waste time, so idled means spent time doing nothing.

clue.text: Poses when taking smack on vacation

indicators.note: a vacated building has been emptied, so the inner letters are removed and only the shell stays

parts.note: as = when, at the time that
a smacker is a kiss, a smack on the lips

explanation.surface: A drug user strikes poses while on holiday with heroin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smack' looks like heroin, but it is a loud kiss.
explanation.definitionFit: To pose a question is to ask it, so poses works as a verb meaning puts forward a query.

clue.text: Regularly attending academic lecture — it's so long

indicators.note: turning up at regular intervals means only every so many letters is present

parts.note: every third letter, starting from the first

explanation.surface: A student goes to a university lecture regularly, complaining it drags on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's so long' sounds like the complaint about the lecture, but 'so long' is the farewell.
explanation.definitionFit: Adieu is a French-borrowed farewell, just as so long is an informal way of saying goodbye.

clue.text: Loveless marriage? Slow down and get off the phone?

indicators.note: love is zero in tennis, so loveless means with the O taken out

parts.note: a marriage is a union
to stall is to hold up or slow progress

explanation.surface: Advice for an unhappy spouse: take things slowly and stop calling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get off the phone' sounds like ending a call, but it means removing an app from the handset.
explanation.definitionFit: Uninstalling software deletes the app from a device, so the program is taken off your mobile.

clue.text: Crew devoured a little exotic sea creature

parts.note: to man a ship is to crew it
devoured = ate

indicators.note: only a little of a word is a small taste of it, its opening letter

parts.note: opening letter

explanation.surface: A ship's crew eats a bit of some strange marine animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crew' looks like a noun, sailors, but it is the verb man.
explanation.definitionFit: The manatee is a large plant-eating aquatic mammal, the sea cow, found in warm coastal waters.

clue.text: Journalist on paper tried

indicators.note: in an across clue one thing on another comes after it, so the first-named piece goes second

parts.note: a paper is a written essay
ED is an editor

explanation.surface: A reporter writing for a newspaper is put on trial.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'on' means after, so the journalist comes after the paper.
explanation.definitionFit: To essay something is a literary verb for to attempt it, so essayed means attempted.
